doc.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Discovering jazz through a friend's father and ear training from Extension
summary: A friend's father played Brubeck, Jamal and others; Dobbins taught himself by ear to decode Extension, finally succeeding in the 1970s.

bands.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Lee Lewis, Little Richard and that kind of stuff. And he had an upright piano in the house. That’s another thing that I read that’s an interesting, worthwhile point too that at the turn of the twentieth century the biggest disseminator of music in America was the piano. So that shows you, you know, people today just push a button and it all just happens for them. We’d get back to his place and sometimes he could actually sit down and play the chorus of the rhythm & blues or boogie woogie piano from his Jerry Lee Lewis record that he had figured out from the record. But his father was a jazz fan and when I was over there one day he played me some records by the Modern Jazz Quartet and Ahmad Jamal’s trio with Vernell Fournier and Israel Crosby And Errol Garner’s “Concert by the Sea.” And Dave Brubeck, well the “Time Out” records but also the “Gone with the Wind” where they play all these songs associated with the south, it’s still one of my favorite records. And I just heard immediately that these people were using all this great chromatic harmony that I loved in classical music and impressionism, and even the Russians again. But they were using it in a conversational way, like a language you know. And from the first time I heard that I had to figure out, how do they do that? So it was not long after that that I got this “Extension” record and as soon as I heard this it just — like I’ve got to figure out what’s going on. I’ve never heard anything like this. I had heard the Thad Jones and Mel Lewis things and I’d heard some Basie and Ellington and Kenton, Maynard Ferguson’s early 60s stuff, Woody Herman. I sat down and some of the harmonies were so unusual that I sometimes couldn’t, wasn’t even sure exactly is that bass note a G or an A flat? Because I don’t have perfect pitch. I put this record on a reel to reel tape and I just couldn’t figure it out. And so I developed a kind of program of ear training for myself where I would take records I really liked with two horns, three horns, four horns, small horn sections, Horace Silver, the Blakey stuff with Freddie Hubbard and Wayne Shorter and Curtis Fuller, and some of the Gerry Mulligan Sextet. He did a couple of records with the sextet, and some of Duke’s things of small groups, and try to figure this stuff out by following the line of each individual horn, you know? And every year or so I’d come back to this record to see if I could get any closer. It was so frustrating. And later on even, when the cassette players came out and you had little portable cassettes. When I was living here I was doing some gigs with Nick Brignola in the mid-80s — no it was in the early 80s — no it must have been the late 70s actually, because I got that record of Clare’s around ’65 or ’66. So it must have been around ’75. We were doing some concerts downstate. They put us up in hotels and so everywhere I went during this period I took my portable cassette player and I would be listening to this record all the time. Finally one night when we were back from a gig I realized that this melody, the notes directly above the bass, it was just basic dominant seventh chords, with roots, thirds and sevenths [plays piano].
